topic: The six fields inside a Bitcoin block header
hook: Every Bitcoin block is judged by just six fields.

scenes.narration: A block header is a compact 80-byte bundle. It holds six fields: version, previous block hash, merkle root, timestamp, difficulty bits and a nonce.
The previous block hash links it to the block before. The merkle root commits to every transaction inside the block.
The nonce is a counter miners keep changing while they search for a hash that meets the target.

cta: Which field surprised you? Tell me in the comments, and the link is in my description.
title: What Is Inside a Bitcoin Block Header?
description_body: A block header is 80 bytes with six fields. See what each one does.

topic: What a merkle root is and why the header holds one
hook: One hash can vouch for thousands of transactions.

scenes.narration: The merkle root is a single hash that commits to every transaction in a block.
That matters because only the 80-byte block header gets hashed for proof of work, not the full list of transactions.
Change any transaction and the merkle root changes, so the header hash changes too. That is how the header protects the whole block.

cta: Did that click for you? Tell me in the comments, and the link is in my description.
title: What Is a Merkle Root in Bitcoin?
description_body: The merkle root lets an 80-byte header commit to every transaction in a block.

topic: Why Bitcoin hashes each header twice
hook: Bitcoin miners hash every header twice, on purpose.

scenes.narration: Each block header is run through SHA-256 twice. That is called double SHA-256.
The result is compared with the network target. It has to be at or below it to count.
Every node uses the same rule, so anyone can repeat the check and get the same answer.

cta: Did you know it was twice? Tell me in the comments, and the link is in my description.
title: Why Bitcoin Hashes Twice (Double SHA-256)
description_body: Each block header is hashed twice and compared with the target.

topic: What the Bitcoin target is
hook: Bitcoin's mining target is just one very large number.

scenes.narration: The target is a 256-bit number that all Bitcoin clients share.
A block's hash has to be lower than or equal to it for the block to be accepted.
The lower the target, the harder it is to generate a block. That is how difficulty works.

title: What Is the Bitcoin Target? Simple Explanation
description_body: The target is a shared 256-bit number. A lower target means harder mining.

topic: The coinbase transaction
hook: The first transaction in every block comes from nowhere.

scenes.narration: Every block starts with a special transaction called the coinbase transaction. It creates the new coins and collects the fees.
It spends no previous output. Its input references nothing.
That is where the miner's reward is claimed. It cannot be more than the subsidy plus fees.

title: What Is the Coinbase Transaction in Bitcoin?
description_body: The first transaction in every block creates new coins and collects fees.

topic: What a satoshi is
hook: Nobody needs a whole bitcoin. Here is the smallest piece.

scenes.narration: One satoshi is the smallest unit of bitcoin. It is one hundred millionth of a single bitcoin.
Block rewards are counted in satoshis. The protocol rounds the subsidy down at that precision.
That rounding is one reason the real cap sits just under twenty-one million.

topic: Myth: mining rewards can be spent immediately
hook: Myth: miners can spend a block reward the second they win it.

scenes.narration: Coinbase outputs cannot be spent until they have received one hundred confirmations.
At roughly one block every ten minutes, that takes many hours.
So a freshly mined reward is locked for a while. Mining income is never instant.

topic: Myth: miners can set any timestamp
hook: Myth: a Bitcoin miner can stamp a block with any time.

scenes.narration: Nodes reject a block header if its timestamp is more than two hours ahead of their own clock.
They also reject it if the timestamp is earlier than the median of the last eleven blocks.
Miners claim a time, but every node checks it. The network enforces the rules, not the miner.
